title: Diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes and nanoparticles

steps.title: Diamond
steps.body: Diamond is pure carbon. Every carbon atom is joined to **four** others by strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional **giant covalent** lattice. So diamond is **very hard**, has a **very high melting point**, and **does not conduct** electricity: all four outer electrons of each atom are used in bonds, so none are free to move.

visuals.alt: A giant covalent lattice such as diamond: every atom bonded to its neighbours

visuals.problem: Explain why diamond is used on the tips of drill bits. (3 marks)

steps.text: Diamond is a giant covalent structure
Each carbon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds in a rigid lattice
So it is very hard and can cut through other materials, and its very high melting point means it survives the heat of drilling

check.prompt: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?

markScheme.description: All electrons in bonds

options: All four outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonds, so none are free to move
Diamond is transparent, and transparent materials cannot carry an electric current
Diamond has no electrons in its outer shells, because they are all shared with other atoms
Diamond is an ionic compound, and ionic compounds cannot conduct when they are solid

steps.title: Graphite
steps.body:
Graphite is also pure carbon, but each atom is bonded to only **three** others, forming flat **layers** of hexagons. Within a layer the covalent bonds are strong; **between** the layers there are **no covalent bonds at all**, only weak forces, so the layers **slide**. That makes graphite soft and slippery: a lubricant, and the "lead" in pencils.

Each carbon has one outer electron left over. It is **delocalised** and can move along the layer, so graphite **conducts electricity**, unusual for a non-metal.

Graphite also has a **very high melting point**: the covalent bonds within the layers are strong and there are a great many of them to break. In one respect graphite is like a metal: it has delocalised electrons, and that is why it conducts.

visuals.alt: Graphite: two layers of hexagons with weak forces between the layers

visuals.problem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but is soft. (4 marks)

steps.text: Each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one electron per atom delocalised
The delocalised electrons move along the layers and carry charge, so graphite conducts
The layers are held together only by weak intermolecular forces
So the layers slide over each other, which makes graphite soft

check.prompt: Which statement explains why graphite conducts electricity?
check.solution: Three bonds, one spare electron, delocalised.

markScheme.description: Three bonds, delocalised fourth electron

options: Each carbon bonds to only three others, and the fourth electron is delocalised
Graphite has layers, and the layers slide
Graphite is a metal, and metals conduct
Graphite has weak bonds, and weak bonds let electrons through

steps.title: Graphene
steps.body: **Graphene** is a single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon hexagons just **one atom thick**. Every atom is covalently bonded to three others, so the sheet is extremely **strong** for its weight, and the delocalised electrons make it a good **conductor**. It was first isolated in Manchester in 2004, using sticky tape to peel layers off graphite. Uses being developed: flexible touch screens, faster electronics, and composites.

visuals.alt: Graphene: a single layer of carbon hexagons

visuals.problem: Graphene is used in flexible touch screens. Give two properties that make it suitable and link each to its structure.

steps.text: Conducts electricity: each carbon has one delocalised electron that moves across the sheet
Strong yet flexible: it is one atom thick, held together by strong covalent bonds across the whole sheet
Transparent: a single layer of atoms lets nearly all the light through

check.solution: Strong covalent bonds across the whole sheet, and no weak layers to separate.

markScheme.description: Strong covalent bonds across the sheet

options: Every carbon is held by strong covalent bonds in a continuous sheet
It has many layers stacked together, each adding to the strength
It has strong intermolecular forces between the carbon atoms
It contains metal atoms that hold the carbon atoms in place

steps.title: Fullerenes and nanotubes
steps.body:
**Fullerenes** are **molecules** of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, mostly hexagons with some pentagons or heptagons. **Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀**, is a hollow ball of 60 atoms, like a football. Because fullerenes are separate molecules, they have low melting points compared with graphite. They can carry drugs into the body, act as lubricants, and as catalysts.

**Carbon nanotubes** are **cylindrical fullerenes**: sheets of graphene rolled into cylinders. They have a very high length to diameter ratio, very **high tensile strength**, and they conduct. They reinforce materials and are used in electronics.

visuals.alt: Buckminsterfullerene, C60: a hollow ball of hexagons and pentagons
A carbon nanotube: a graphene sheet rolled into a cylinder

check.prompt: Which is a use of carbon nanotubes?
check.solution: Strong along their length and light: composites and electronics.

markScheme.description: Reinforcing materials

options: Reinforcing materials, because of their high tensile strength
Making pencil leads, because they are soft and slippery
Cutting glass, because they are the hardest form of carbon
Making jewellery, because they sparkle in the light

steps.title: Surface area to volume ratio
steps.body:
Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nanometres across (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m); the smallest contain only a few hundred atoms. Their special properties come from having a huge **surface area compared with their volume**.

Because so much of a nanoparticle is surface, nanoparticles can behave **differently from the same material in bulk**: gold nanoparticles are red, not gold, and a metal that is unreactive as a lump can be an excellent catalyst as nanoparticles. For scale, a single atom is about 0.1 nm across, so a 10 nm nanoparticle is roughly 100 atoms wide: far bigger than one atom, far smaller than anything you can see.

visuals.problem: Compare the surface area to volume ratio of a 10 nm cube and a 1 nm cube

steps.text: 10 nm cube: surface area 6 × 10² = 600 nm², volume 10³ = 1000 nm³, ratio 0.6
1 nm cube: surface area 6 × 1² = 6 nm², volume 1 nm³, ratio 6
Divide the side by 10 and the ratio goes up by 10

check.prompt: What happens to the surface area to volume ratio as a particle gets smaller?
check.solution: Smaller particles have far more surface for the same amount of material.

markScheme.description: Increases

options: It increases
It decreases
It stays the same
It becomes zero

steps.title: Using nanoparticles, and the risks
steps.body:
All that surface is what makes them useful: a tiny mass can do a big job:

- **Catalysts**: less material for the same reacting surface.
- **Medicine**: carrying drugs to specific cells.
- **Sun creams**: nano titanium dioxide blocks UV but looks clear on skin.
- **Deodorants and socks**: silver nanoparticles kill bacteria.
- **Electronics**: ever smaller components.

The possible downsides are not fully known. Nanoparticles may be absorbed into the body or washed into the environment, and their long-term effects on cells and wildlife are still being studied. Exam questions ask for a **balanced** answer: benefit, risk, and "more research is needed".

check.prompt: Why do nanoparticle catalysts need less material than ordinary catalysts?
check.solution: Catalysis happens on the surface, and nanoparticles are nearly all surface.

markScheme.description: High surface area to volume ratio

options: Their high surface area to volume ratio gives a large reacting surface for a small mass
They are stronger than ordinary catalysts, so they do not wear away during the reaction
They have more electrons per atom, so they can take part in more reactions at once
They are heavier than ordinary catalysts, so a smaller number of particles is needed

visuals.problem: Evaluate the use of titanium dioxide nanoparticles in sun cream

steps.text: Benefit: blocks UV well and, being so small, looks clear on the skin instead of white
Concern: nanoparticles might be absorbed through skin or wash into the sea, and the effects are not fully known
Judgement: useful, but more research is needed on long-term safety

steps.title: Grade 9: the same element, four structures
steps.body:
Diamond, graphite, graphene, and fullerenes are all pure carbon, and every property difference comes from **how many bonds each atom makes and how the atoms are arranged**. Four bonds in 3D: hard, insulating (diamond). Three bonds in layers: soft, conducting (graphite). One layer alone: strong, conducting (graphene). Closed molecules: low melting points (fullerenes).

Top answers also keep the size classes straight: **coarse** particles, **PM10** (dust), 2,500 to 10,000 nm; **fine** particles, **PM2.5**, 100 to 2,500 nm; **nanoparticles** 1 to 100 nm.

visuals.problem: Explain why C60 has a low melting point but graphite does not

steps.text: C60 is a molecule; graphite is a giant covalent structure
Melting C60 overcomes weak intermolecular forces between molecules
Melting graphite breaks strong covalent bonds within the layers

check.prompt: Which property difference is explained by the number of bonds each carbon atom makes?
check.solution: Four bonds leave no spare electron; three leave one delocalised electron.

markScheme.description: Conduction: four bonds versus three

options: Diamond does not conduct but graphite does
Diamond forms deep underground at high pressure but graphite does not
Diamond is rarer than graphite
Both have high melting points

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Diamond: four bonds per atom, rigid 3D lattice, very hard, no conduction.
- Graphite: three bonds per atom, layers that slide, delocalised electrons conduct.
- Graphene: one layer of graphite, very strong, conducts.
- Fullerenes: hollow carbon molecules (C₆₀, nanotubes); low melting points because they are molecules; nanotubes have high tensile strength.
- Nanoparticles: 1 to 100 nm; huge surface area to volume ratio; used in catalysts, medicine, sun cream; risks still being researched.

questions.prompt: In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
questions.solution: Four bonds, in a rigid three-dimensional lattice.

questions.prompt: In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
questions.solution: Three bonds in flat layers of hexagons. The fourth electron is delocalised.
One layer of hexagons, lifted off graphite.

options: a single layer of graphite, one atom thick
a hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms
a form of diamond

questions.prompt: Why is graphite soft and slippery?
questions.solution: Strong within the layers, weak between them. Pencils work because layers slide off onto the paper.

markScheme.description: Weak forces between layers, layers slide

options: The layers are held by weak intermolecular forces, so they slide over each other
The covalent bonds within each layer are weak, so the layers break apart easily
The carbon atoms are far apart in every direction, so there is little holding them
Its delocalised electrons act as a lubricant between the carbon atoms

questions.prompt: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
questions.solution: Three bonds use three electrons. The fourth is delocalised, so graphite conducts like a metal along its layers.

markScheme.description: One delocalised electron per carbon in graphite

options: In graphite each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move along the layers; in diamond all four outer electrons are in bonds
Graphite is a metal, so it has a sea of delocalised electrons; diamond is a non-metal, so it has none
In diamond the electrons are locked inside the nucleus; in graphite the weak bonds let electrons escape from the atoms
Graphite contains ions that can move between the layers; diamond has no ions because all its atoms are neutral

questions.solution: A rigid three-dimensional network of strong covalent bonds resists any change of shape.

markScheme.description: Rigid lattice of strong covalent bonds

options: Each carbon is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds in a rigid 3D lattice
Each carbon is joined to three others in layers that are held together by strong forces
Its atoms are held together by very strong intermolecular forces in every direction
It is a metal, so its layers of ions are locked in place by delocalised electrons

questions.solution: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes. C₆₀ is the football-shaped one.

options: a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms arranged in hexagons and pentagons
a giant covalent structure of 60 layers of carbon atoms in hexagons
a single flat sheet of 60 carbon atoms arranged in hexagons

questions.prompt: There are 10ⁿ nanometres in one metre. What is the value of n?
questions.solution: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, so one metre is 10⁹ nanometres and n = 9.

questions.prompt: Graphite is used as a lubricant and in pencils, and also as electrodes in electrolysis. Explain how the structure and bonding of graphite make it suitable for both uses.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Both uses need to be linked back to a named feature of the structure.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about layers, weak forces between them, and delocalised electrons, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of layers, weak forces between them, and delocalised electrons with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of layers, weak forces between them, and delocalised electrons using the correct terms

criteria.text: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms, each bonded to three others by strong covalent bonds
There are only weak intermolecular forces between the layers
So the layers slide over each other, making graphite soft and slippery, good for lubrication and marking paper
Each carbon has one electron not used in bonding, which is delocalised
These delocalised electrons can move along the layers, so graphite conducts electricity, good for electrodes
Graphite also has a very high melting point because the covalent bonds within layers are strong, so it survives the conditions in electrolysis

questions.modelAnswer: Graphite is made of layers of carbon atoms. Within each layer every carbon is joined to three others by strong covalent bonds in hexagons, but between the layers there are only weak intermolecular forces. The layers can slide over each other, which makes graphite soft and slippery: ideal for a lubricant and for leaving marks on paper. Each carbon uses only three of its four outer electrons in bonds. The fourth is delocalised and free to move along the layers, so graphite conducts electricity and can be used as an electrode. Its strong covalent bonds also give it a very high melting point, so it stands up to hot electrolysis cells.

questions.prompt: Graphene has a high melting point and conducts electricity, but it is not a metal. Which statement explains the conduction?
questions.solution: Same reason as graphite: one spare electron per atom, delocalised.

markScheme.description: One delocalised electron per carbon

options: Each carbon uses three electrons in covalent bonds, and the fourth is delocalised across the sheet
Graphene contains positive carbon ions held in a sea of delocalised electrons, like a metal
The weak intermolecular forces between the carbon atoms let electrons hop from atom to atom
Graphene is ionic, so its charged particles are free to move across the sheet

questions.prompt: C₆₀ has a much lower melting point than graphite. Why?
questions.solution: Fullerenes are molecules. Melting only overcomes the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.

markScheme.description: Molecules with weak intermolecular forces versus giant structure

options: C₆₀ is made of separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces, whereas graphite is a giant covalent structure
The covalent bonds in C₆₀ are much weaker than those in graphite because the ball shape strains them
C₆₀ contains far fewer carbon atoms in total, so there are fewer bonds to break when it melts
C₆₀ is ionic, and ionic compounds always melt at lower temperatures than covalent ones

questions.prompt: A cube has sides of 1 cm. It is cut into cubes with sides of 1 mm. Calculate how many times greater the total surface area of the small cubes is compared with the original cube, and explain why this matters for nanoparticles used as catalysts.
questions.solution: Combines a calculation with the surface area to volume idea and its consequence.

markScheme.description: Original surface area 6 cm²
1000 small cubes
Total 60 cm², 10 times greater
High surface area to volume ratio
Less catalyst needed

criteria.text: Surface area of original cube = 6 × 1² = 6 cm²
Total surface area = 1000 × 6 × 0.1² = 60 cm², so 10 times greater
Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio
So a much smaller mass of catalyst gives the same surface for reactions, which is cheaper and uses less material

questions.modelAnswer: The original cube has surface area 6 × 1 cm × 1 cm = 6 cm². Cutting each side into 10 gives 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cubes, each with surface area 6 × 0.1 cm × 0.1 cm = 0.06 cm², so 60 cm² in total, which is 10 times greater. Every time the side length is divided by 10, the surface area to volume ratio goes up 10 times. Nanoparticles are so small that their surface area to volume ratio is enormous, so a tiny mass of nanoparticle catalyst provides a very large surface for the reaction. Less catalyst is needed, which saves money and resources.

questions.prompt: Nanoparticles of silver are added to some socks to kill bacteria. Suggest a possible disadvantage that should be investigated before this becomes widespread.
questions.solution: The specification expects a balanced view: benefits, plus possible risks that are still being studied.

markScheme.description: Unknown effects on health and environment

options: Nanoparticles may be washed out, enter the environment, and their effects on living things are not yet fully understood
Silver is a metal, so the nanoparticles will rust in the wash and stain the socks and the washing machine
Nanoparticles are too heavy for fabric, so the socks would become uncomfortable to wear over time
Silver nanoparticles conduct electricity, so the socks could give the wearer an electric shock

questions.prompt: A particle has a diameter of 1200 nm. Which is it?
questions.solution: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm; fine particles (PM2.5) 100 to 2500 nm; coarse particles (PM10, dust) 2500 to 10,000 nm. At 1200 nm this sits inside the fine range.

markScheme.description: Fine particle

options: A fine particle (PM2.5)
A nanoparticle
A coarse particle (dust)
An atom

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped nanoparticle of side 10 nm has a surface area to volume ratio of 0.6 per nm. What is the ratio for a cube of side 2 nm? Give your answer in the same units.
questions.solution: For a cube of side s the ratio is 6s² ÷ s³ = 6 ÷ s. For s = 2 nm that is 3 per nm, five times the 10 nm value. Halving the size doubles the ratio; dividing it by five multiplies the ratio by five.

markScheme.description: Ratio = 6 ÷ side, or surface area 24 nm² and volume 8 nm³

questions.prompt: Graphene is being added to sports equipment such as tennis rackets and bicycle frames. Explain, in terms of its structure and bonding, why graphene is suitable for this use.
questions.skill: linking graphene structure to a use
questions.solution: Three structure-to-property links: thin and light, covalently bonded across the sheet, so strong.

markScheme.description: One atom thick: very little mass
Strong covalent bonds across the sheet
Hard to break: high tensile strength
Strength added for almost no weight

criteria.text: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, one atom thick, so it adds very little mass
Every carbon atom is bonded to three others by strong covalent bonds across the whole sheet
Strong covalent bonds are hard to break, so the sheet has a very high tensile strength
So it adds strength to the racket or frame for almost no extra weight

questions.modelAnswer: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, only one atom thick, so adding it to a racket or frame adds almost no mass. Within the sheet every carbon atom is joined to three others by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network of hexagons. Those bonds are very hard to break, so graphene has a very high tensile strength for its thickness. Mixed into the material, it makes the equipment stronger and stiffer for almost no extra weight.

examTechnique.body: Questions on the forms of carbon always come back to bonds per atom and the forces between the parts. Say how many bonds each carbon makes, name the structure, then explain the property. For nanoparticles, be ready to calculate a surface area to volume ratio and to give a balanced view of benefits and risks.
examinerErrors: Saying graphite conducts "because it is a metal" or "because it has layers". It conducts because of delocalised electrons.

Saying the layers in graphite are held by weak covalent bonds. The bonds within a layer are strong; between the layers there are no covalent bonds at all, only weak forces, and "no covalent bonds between the layers" is the specification's own wording.
Calling C₆₀ a giant covalent structure. It is a molecule.
Mixing up the size classes: nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm, not micrometres.
Giving only benefits of nanoparticles when asked to evaluate.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states the number of bonds per carbon and the resulting structure before explaining a property, distinguishes molecules (fullerenes) from giant structures, can calculate and interpret a surface area to volume ratio, and evaluates nanoparticle uses with both benefits and unknown risks.
